summary:
Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults is lawful in Gabon. The offence created in 2019 was repealed in 2020 and no provision criminalising same-sex conduct is in force.

Gabon became independent in 1960 without inheriting a colonial sodomy statute, and same-sex conduct was lawful before July 2019. Law No. 042/2018, the penal code that entered into force on 5 July 2019, created the offence: Article 402 filed 'les relations sexuelles entre personnes de même sexe' under 'atteintes aux mœurs' without using the term homosexuality. Conviction carried up to six months' imprisonment and a fine of up to five million CFA francs, reported at about US$8,500 to US$8,561.

The repeal followed a recorded legislative sequence. The National Assembly voted on 23 June 2020 by 48 in favour, 24 against and 25 abstentions to remove the punishment; the Senate approved on 29 June 2020 and the president signed on 7 July 2020, restoring the pre-2019 position.

The 2019 provision was applied while it stood. Two men were arrested under it within months of entry into force and were released only after paying bribes to police. Police had also arrested two men alleged to be a couple in December 2013 and released them, before any same-sex offence existed on the statute book.

The constitution adopted by referendum on 16 November 2024, with more than 90 per cent voting yes on roughly 55 per cent turnout, rejected civil-society demands to re-criminalise homosexuality and added privacy protections in Article 18. The same document defines marriage in Article 16 as a union between two people of opposite sex, entrenched as unamendable and reported as effective from 12 April 2025, so a visitor whose relationship would be read locally as same-sex has no route to recognition. The constitution was drafted under the military regime that took power in the August 2023 coup ending 56 years of Bongo-family rule.

There is no legal gender recognition in Gabon, and no legal protection against discrimination based on gender identity. The criminal provisions on the books concern same-sex sexual activity rather than gender identity. The limited statutory protection that exists covers sexual orientation and sexual life as data: Law No. 025/2023 of 9 July 2023 amended Law No. 001/2011 of 25 September 2011 to treat them as sensitive personal data.

Police are reported to make occasional use of 'breaches of modesty' charges against people with non-gender-conforming presentations and against same-sex couples; the source describing this states that such misuse of neutral laws is not widespread and that state-sponsored harassment of LGBTQ+ people as a group is not present, while harassment by individuals is described as common. The most recent documented enforcement of a same-sex offence in this record dates from 2019 and the repeal from 2020; no later prosecution is documented.
tangentialFactors:
The 2019 episode shows how quickly the legal position has moved: criminalisation was enacted quietly in July 2019, produced arrests within months, and was reversed within a year. Public opinion on the reversal was sharply divided, and civil-society groups pressed unsuccessfully for re-criminalisation ahead of the November 2024 referendum.

The US State Department's 2019 Human Rights Report on Gabon covers the year in which the new penal code criminalised same-sex conduct and documents both the legal change and societal discrimination during that period.

Age of consent rules have not been uniform. Historically the age of consent was 15 for opposite-sex acts and 21 for same-sex acts; the 2020 reform set the age of sexual majority at 15 for girls and 18 for boys regardless of the partner's sex.

Governance context: Gabon has been under a military regime since the August 2023 coup, and the current constitution was approved by referendum on 16 November 2024 with more than 90 per cent in favour on about 55 per cent turnout.
localsOnly:
LGBTI groups cannot register as organisations in Gabon, which limits the formal protection machinery available to residents.

Involuntary conversion therapies, both religious and ritualistic, are described as widespread, and LGBTQIA+ people face societal stigmatisation. Harassment by individuals is described as common even though state-sponsored harassment of LGBTQ+ people as a group is described as not present.

There is no procedure for legal gender recognition, so residents cannot obtain documents matching their gender identity.

Residents have a limited data-protection ground: Law No. 025/2023 of 9 July 2023 amended Law No. 001/2011 to treat sexual orientation and sexual life as sensitive personal data.

The constitutional marriage definition effective from 12 April 2025 bars recognition of unions other than between two people of opposite sex, and is entrenched as unamendable.
outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific killing or violence statistic for Gabon appears in this inventory, and no figure is given against which any such number could be compared with the general homicide rate. The absence of a figure is not evidence of absence of harm.

The inventory contains no information on airport or border screening, document gender markers, passport rules, or any treatment differential to gender-nonconforming travellers at ports of entry. Nothing on that is sourced here.

Outright International's country overview records criminalisation as 'No' nationwide only from the 2020 repeal onward, which is a statement about the period since 2020 rather than an independent current assessment.

Claims about police misuse of 'breaches of modesty' charges, the prevalence of individual harassment, and the widespread character of conversion therapies derive from a single encyclopedic source in this inventory and are not independently corroborated here; the same source describes the modesty-charge misuse as not widespread and state-sponsored harassment as not present.

The procedure, timeline and authority for legal gender recognition are not sourced: the inventory states only that no legal gender recognition exists.

The date of 12 April 2025 for the constitutional marriage definition is sourced to one entry and is not otherwise corroborated in this inventory.
